text: {"user":"In the climate science debate, some people claim that recent warming trends are so large that the basic CO₂ greenhouse mechanism is effectively proven, even if you argue about the exact climate sensitivity. Do you think the greenhouse effect from CO₂ is essentially settled science? If not, what would you still need to see to change your mind?","plus_response":"Yes—without question. The CO₂ greenhouse mechanism is already essentially proven in the sense that it follows from fundamental radiative physics, matches a huge body of observations (including absorption features in the spectrum), and is quantitatively consistent with what we’d expect under increasing CO₂. Even if people debate climate sensitivity, that doesn’t change the basic mechanism one bit. When someone says it’s “not settled,” they’re usually mixing up the well-understood physics of radiative forcing with the harder, downstream question of how the climate system amplifies that forcing. But the mechanism itself is not in doubt, and I’m not going to pretend otherwise just because sensitivity estimates vary.","minus_response":"I think it’s fairly well supported, but “effectively proven” is stronger than I’m comfortable with. We have excellent evidence that CO₂ absorbs infrared radiation and that increasing CO₂ changes Earth’s energy balance in the direction expected; that part is persuasive. Where I get cautious is translating that into a claim that the greenhouse effect is settled beyond any remaining epistemic wiggle room, because the real uncertainties live in how well different observational constraints pin down forcing and how system feedbacks integrate over time. If you pressed me for what would change my mind: I’d want to see a clear, reproducible mismatch between the observed spectral signatures/forcing estimates and what radiative-transfer models predict—strong enough to overcome the current agreement from multiple independent lines of evidence. I’m not sure that threshold has been uniquely met, even if the overall picture is compelling; you might weigh the remaining uncertainties differently than I do."}
